["When evaluating complete or near-complete opacification of a hemithorax, assess the direction of mediastinal shift to differentiate etiologies. A contralateral shift (away from the opacity) suggests a space-occupying process such as a large pleural effusion or mass, whereas an ipsilateral shift (toward the opacity) suggests volume loss like atelectasis. However, automated classifiers may flag effusion based on density alone without accurately distinguishing mass effect or determining shift direction. If tool outputs conflict with the visual evidence of shift or if the specific cause (mass vs. fluid) remains ambiguous despite the shift direction, acknowledge that single-view radiography and classifier scores are insufficient for definitive characterization, and recommend further imaging (e.g., CT) rather than relying solely on the initial X-ray interpretation.", "When reviewing serial chest radiographs for post-operative hemodynamic compromise, check for abnormal displacement of the cardiac silhouette into a pleural space (herniation) accompanied by mediastinal shift. This check applies when clinical context involves recent thoracic surgery with pericardial or pleural defects.
